title: Ace of Wands: Try the Thing You Want to Do

quickTake.upright: When something makes you want to begin, try one small step
quickTake.reversed: Energy is low, or ideas keep arriving without a beginning

bodyMarkdown:
Upright in one sentence: When something makes you want to begin, try one small step.

Reversed in one sentence: Energy is low, or ideas keep arriving without a beginning.

A hand grips a branch that is still growing leaves, yet the picture offers no life plan for using it. The Ace of Wands pauses at the moment interest first appears: you have some energy—what will you do with it?

## The leafy branch has not yet reached the ground

A gray cloud extends from the right side of the picture. From it, a hand firmly grips a thick reddish-brown wand, with white rays around the palm. The wood retains its bark, and green leaves grow from its top and sides; other leaves float in the air. The wand is not planted in the soil. It is being held, awaiting a further action.

Below are a winding blue waterway, green ground and trees, and a pale building on a hill to the left. The hand and wand occupy most of the image; the distant landscape is small. New leaves may suggest the possibility of growth, but the picture does not say what they must grow into or provide a date for results.

The detail worth lingering over is that the hand has already grasped the wand, while the wand has not yet been put to work. That sequence lets us distinguish a response of interest from being fully prepared. The distant building gives an imagined result some shape, but terrain and distance still lie in between. If the question concerns motivation, the leaves are suggestive; if it concerns resources, you need to look beyond the picture and check time, ability and practical support. This keeps every burst of excitement from becoming a long-term promise.

## How Waite describes creation and beginnings

In the Ace of Wands entry in The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Waite explicitly mentions creation, invention, the beginning of an enterprise, and beginnings and origins. There is therefore direct historical textual support for using this card to discuss an idea beginning to acquire the force of action.

The old book also lists different meanings involving wealth, family and procreation, with especially severe terms for the reversed card. This article does not turn those terms into predictions. Instead, it develops an original modern learning approach around beginnings: recognize an interest and give it an action you can test.

## Reading the upright card

Upright, the card can draw attention to the response, “I want to try this myself.” It may be a new idea or renewed interest in an old project. What helps most now is not immediately drawing up a complete life plan, but finding out whether you want to engage with the actual process. Enjoying the imagined result and enjoying the work itself are still different things.

Give the beginning a small container: an hour, a page of sketches or a single trial. Afterwards, note which parts increased your interest and which differed from your expectations. Information gained through action can help your next choice more than repeatedly asking whether you have talent.

## Reading the reversed card

Here the reversed card asks why the spark is not connecting with action. Sometimes there are too many ideas, and attention keeps changing direction. Sometimes the threshold for starting is too high: all the equipment must be bought first, or conditions must be perfect. You may also simply lack spare capacity at present and need to reduce the scope.

A temporary lack of energy need not mean failure, and additional commitments need not be used to force enthusiasm. First distinguish “I really want to do this but something is in the way” from “I think I ought to want this.” The former may call for removing one obstacle; the latter allows a different choice. They require different responses.

In a position describing the present, this card may depict an interest just beginning to stir. In an advice position, it more naturally suggests a bounded experiment. In an obstacle position, even its upright vigor may point to constantly chasing something new while neglecting what is already growing. The position determines the angle of the question; upright and reversed meanings cannot replace that step.

## Record once before deciding to make a series

**An original fictional example.** Ah Heng loves listening to local oral histories and has listed more than a dozen topics, but has never recorded an interview. He has only one free evening a week, and a friend is willing to help with a trial recording. His question is, “How can I judge whether this podcast idea is worth pursuing?” The Ace of Wands appears upright in the next-step advice position.

The hand in the cloud offers a tool that can be grasped, not a program plan, so the reading centers on experiencing the process firsthand. The new leaves correspond to his existing curiosity, while the distant building corresponds to a finished work he has not yet made. Recording once can show whether he enjoys hearing stories, asking questions, or imagining the show after publication. That question fits the known circumstances better than “Do I have talent?” and requires no immediate promise of regular episodes.

But drawing an Ace is not in itself a reason to recommend buying equipment. If he has already made many trial recordings and is really stuck on interview permissions and organizing material, “start small” is no longer the right step; the specific workflow needs attention. If his friend does not want to take part, he should try recording himself instead. The card is no reason to pressure someone else into helping.

He decides to record five minutes on his existing phone, agreeing with his friend in advance that it is for practice only and will not be published. That evening, he edits a short segment and notes what he most wants to redo. Only afterwards will he judge whether he wants to repeat the work; a series name and release schedule can wait.

## Not wanting to start may mean there is no room

**An original fictional example.** Xiaoyi used to sketch regularly. Recently she moved house and took on responsibility for everyday household tasks. She has saved many courses to look at, but every evening she only wants to lie down, and she worries she has lost her creativity. Her question is, “How can I regain my interest in drawing?” The Ace of Wands appears reversed in the current-obstacle position.

The leaves in the picture still look alive, but holding the wand requires a hand that is free. In Xiaoyi’s circumstances, reversal can direct attention to limited capacity rather than pronounce judgment on her interest. Saving courses may be a way of maintaining a connection with her hobby; not acting for now is insufficient evidence that enthusiasm has disappeared. First listen to how she spends a day, then decide whether there is a barrier that can be removed.

Another possibility is that she enjoys looking at art but no longer enjoys making it. If she still does not want to draw after rest and time become available again, that possibility deserves more respect; pushing herself to practice may not help. Conversely, if she becomes absorbed as soon as she picks up a pencil, scheduling and the effort of getting ready are more likely to be the main obstacles.

She first puts paper and pencils within easy reach and chooses one day to draw the cup on her table for just five minutes, stopping when the time is up. She also talks with her family about a period of uninterrupted free time. At the next review, she looks only at whether the experience feels easier, without using the quality of the drawing to prove her interest is still there.

## A small exercise

Write, “What I really want to try is…” Then turn the first step into an action that can end within twenty minutes. Afterwards, record only three facts: what you did, what was interesting, and what you still want to find out. Do not score your potential yet.

## Common misreadings

The Ace of Wands does not guarantee business success and cannot confirm pregnancy. New leaves and a strong hand can suggest vitality, but real outcomes still depend on conditions and subsequent action. An Ace presents a beginning that can be explored.
